“UKMTO is struggling to accurately report true number of attacks with majority of vessels attacked refusing to report to UKMTO,” the maritime security organisation stated. It said it was aware of more incidents in the waterway via other sources but could not verify them due to a lack of information.
The same pattern has been true for the first half of October. The month has seen the highest number of ship attacks since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
Of the 12 vessels that were confirmed attacked, the organisation said half continued to their destination or reached port. One sank, two were disabled, and three were either damaged or had an unconfirmed outcome.
The UKMTO also reported a new type of attack on Saturday. The master of a tanker said their vessel was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade (RPG) fired from a small boat 78 nautical miles (equivalent to about 144km) northeast of Saudi Arabia’s city of Jubail, Eastern province, resulting in damage to the aft port quarter.
In recent months, the US has managed to increase energy transits through the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways through a shuttle system coordinated with Arab powers. But volumes have oscillated weekly due to rising Iranian attacks.
Oil flows through Hormuz were at 11.6 million barrels per day (bpd) over the seven days to October 13. This was about 68 percent of the 17.1 million bpd pre-war baseline, according to Kpler figures.
On Friday, Brent crude also touched $110 a barrel for the first time since May in light of ongoing attacks. The situation has been exacerbated by the Iran-aligned Houthis’ attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and their capture of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Expectations that the conflict between the US and Iran was escalating have also impacted prices.
The US military has provided a starkly different outlook on the situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for roughly a fifth of global oil and natural gas flows before the war began.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Brad Cooper claimed in a video message late Friday that despite the Iranian attacks, 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz over the past week.
“Let me be clear: The Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran,” he said, attributing the greatly increased ship attacks to “desperation” by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The US military also claimed that it continues to prevent Iranian exports and imports via its southern ports through an “ironclad” naval blockade. It claims the blockade has cost Iran $25bn in oil export income, and that the US has recently seized $350m in Iranian cryptocurrency financing.
The UKMTO report said total outbound transit over the last seven days was 125 ships, with total inbound transits standing at 129. Over the week, most transits by the Western security agency were for dry bulk cargo, followed by tanker products and general cargo.
Tehran has not provided exact figures on how many vessels have been attacked, or how many are passing through the Hormuz, although it has said Washington is exaggerating numbers to project success of its naval campaign.
It comes as two vessels were reportedly hit by naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz this week, with the US and Iran offering contradictory claims about the situation.
The IRGC has increasingly reported that vessels are hitting mines across the strategic waterway, which it says remains unsafe for vessels which do not coordinate with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority, an entity set up during the war to manage passage through the Hormuz.
The latest claim came on Saturday, when the IRGC said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil caught fire after striking a mine while moving through an “unauthorised” route.
Iran’s state-run Press TV shared footage it says showed the tanker on fire. But CENTCOM said it had cleared the strait of naval mines, and that vessels are being struck by projectiles.
The latest incident “fact-checked” by the US military was on Thursday, when it said a civilian container ship, the M/V GFS Pride, was hit by an IRGC projectile, not by a mine as the Iranians had claimed. The vessel sank as it was being towed to shore.
The US has refrained from responding to any of the recent vessel attacks, but there are concerns that Washington could escalate the war after the November 3 midterm elections.
Diplomacy has not fully halted, with messages continuing to be relayed between the two parties by regional mediators like Pakistan, Qatar and others. But no breakthrough in talks is expected any time soon.
President Donald Trump has reportedly ordered the US military to remain prepared for launching bigger attacks after the elections. Those attacks could potentially include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs”, according to US media.
But Tehran has signalled that it intends to continue the attacks, with acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn Reza saying on Saturday that it will be Iranian missiles, not US bombs, that determine the future of the war.
“Your bombs will explode elsewhere; in your global reputation, the US economy, and even your electoral calculations,” he was quoted as saying by state media.

articles.title: US Special Operations adopts new half-mask and goggles
articles.snippet: Avon Protection's MITR half-mask and goggle system is designed to protect wearers from dangerous chemicals and toxic substances in the atmosphere.
articles.full_text:
U.S. Special Operations forces will adopt a new face and breathing protection system after the Pentagon and Avon Protection announced a contract on Oct. 9.
The MITR half-mask and goggle system is designed to protect wearers from dangerous chemicals and toxic substances in the atmosphere, including lead powder from gunfire, ballistics and poisonous substances like fentanyl.
Casey Galligan, Avon’s senior director for the U.S. Homeland Security and the Department of Defense, told Defense News that fentanyl and chemicals found in drug labs are now part of a wide array of hazards that special warfare operators must guard against, in addition to biological weapons and other breathing hazards.
“Precursor drug chemicals now are a huge issue that are just as dangerous as a chemical hazard,” Galligan said. “As an operator, every day you’re doing something quasi-dangerous, particularly those at the frontline doing maneuver. This is not meant to replace a full-face respirator. A split system gives you options.”
The half-mask system walks the line between an N-95 disposable mask and a heavy, full-face respirator. The goggles and half-mask can be worn linked together or separated, giving operators a lightweight option that will give them eye and breathing protection as needed without requiring them to carry heavy full-face respirator masks.
The MITR features positive pressure-sealed goggles to stop hazardous chemicals from getting in around its edges. The system features sweat drainage outlets inside the goggles and blows cool air into them from both sides, preventing lens fogging.
A former U.S. Army Green Beret, Galligan said the system provides safety against toxic materials while allowing wearers to breathe easier — literally.
“If you don’t always want to be wearing a full-face respirator, and you’re worried about different levels of threats, this is a half-pound and easy to put on. You can wear it with a head harness or with helmet attachments,” he explained.
Half-mask systems are not new, but the MITR system has evolved constantly to incorporate new evolutions in technology to reach its current capabilities.
“We’ve been going through iterations and continuing to improve it,” said Galligan, adding that the U.S. is joining Canada and another FVEY nation in purchasing the system.
Elite warfare units of U.S. Special Operations are already wearing the new half-mask and goggles in the field, he disclosed.
“We’ve fielded it to units already. Some are en route right now, being delivered,” Galligan said. “The feedback I get talking with end users is pretty amazing.”
The Defense Department’s decision to equip SOCOM operators with improved breathing equipment follows a November 2025 report, called the SOF Cancer Study, which revealed that SOF operators face an 18% higher risk of cancer than non-SOF personnel due to hazardous materials in their environments that they are exposed to constantly in the line of duty.
Shifting to a half-mask system could mark the dawn of a new era in how military service members approach facial protection overall.
“When you see the tip of the spear using it, it’s going to make it a lot more acceptable,” Galligan said.
Zita Ballinger Fletcher previously served as editor of Military History Quarterly and Vietnam magazines and as the historian of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. She holds an M.A. with distinction in military history.

articles.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
articles.snippet: Ukraine said on Wednesday that SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon.
While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
WHAT IS STARLINK?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
WHAT IS STARSHIELD?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported.
SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defense ministry has told Reuters.
Other U.S. partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

articles.title: US Army’s 8th Psychological Operations Group inactivated
articles.snippet: The Army's 8th Psychological Operations Group inactivated as the service reshapes its PSYOP and information warfare forces to counter global adversaries.
articles.full_text:
The Army officially inactivated the 8th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) in a ceremony at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, on Sept. 29.
“I could not be prouder of the men and women that stand before us today and those that came before us to inactivate the unit,” Col. Robert Cusick, the group’s commanding officer, said. “8th PSYOP Group introduced new concepts that will remain for years to come.”
8th POG, nicknamed the “Phantom Knights,” was formally activated on Nov. 16, 2013, after operating provisionally for two years. It was one of four Army PSYOP groups, including the active-duty 4th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) and the Army Reserve’s 2nd and 7th Psychological Operations Groups.
The term “inactivation” signifies that the group is being decommissioned for an indeterminate period during some form of restructuring and reorganization — not necessarily that it is being deactivated or dissolved.
The 8th POG included the 3rd PSYOP Battalion (Airborne) and the 9th PSYOP Battalion (Airborne). The 3rd POB influences print, radio and broadcast information operations around the world, while the 9th POB is typically involved in operations like dropping leaflets and cultivating local communities where Special Forces may be operating.
The Information Warfare Center, organized in 2020, was also under the aegis of the 8th PG. The IWC combines intelligence operations and information warfare specifically for Army Special Forces.
The inactivation comes just two months after the Army activated Delta Company, 7th Psychological Operations Battalion. The 7th was previously assigned to the 4th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) but is now under the 3rd Special Forces Group (Airborne). That group is focused on psychological operations primarily under U.S. Africa Command’s purview.
Some military officials and analysts have argued that the U.S. needs to overhaul its approach to psychological operations and information warfare groups — hence the Delta Company activation and the retirement of the 8th POG.
“What is most concerning is not simply that adversaries invest in information warfare, but that they can often employ it faster and more coherently than we can respond,” Maj. Ryan Walters, an active-duty U.S. Army Psychological Operations officer, wrote in Small Wars Journal in January. “In practice, adversaries win by compressing the time between sensing, shaping, and exploiting, while U.S. forces remain constrained by approval latency, fragmented execution, and inconsistent assessment. The result is a temporal mismatch in which effects arrive after decisions are already made.”

articles.title: Arizona Guard first to field Gray Eagle 25M drone
articles.snippet: The state will receive 12 of the unmanned aircraft systems by the end of 2029.
articles.full_text:
The Arizona National Guard will become the first state to establish a unit equipped with the unmanned aircraft system, or UAS, known as the Gray Eagle 25M.
According to Monday’s announcement by General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, which manufactures the aircraft, the Arizona Guard will receive eight Gray Eagle 25Ms by September 2027 and four more by the end of 2029.
Patrick Shortsleeve, the company’s vice president of Defense Department strategic development, called the aircraft “an integral part of the Army Aviation team” as it works closely with advanced autonomy and manned rotary-wing systems to outpace threats.
“The Gray Eagle has a proven record of performance with 1 million hours of safe operations, including automatic takeoff and landing capability,” he said. “When you factor in its extensive capabilities, the Gray Eagle is a cost-effective UAS that excels as an enabler for Fires, Maneuver, Network, and Intelligence operations.”
The National Guard’s goal, according to General Atomics, is to create a UAS company in each of its eight infantry divisions. The Arizona Guard is part of the 40th Infantry Division, which covers 11 other states or territories and is headquartered in California.
“Once fully operational, the Gray Eagle 25M can deploy in support of global missions for Combatant Command (COCOM) commanders and defend against threats in the Western Hemisphere,” the company said, adding that currently, Congress has funded three Gray Eagle 25M guard units.
The Gray Eagle 25M, the newest edition of the decades-old Gray Eagle UAS, made its first flight in December 2023. That same month, the federal government awarded General Atomics a $389 million contract to develop the system.
According to the company, the “M” in the 25M stands for “modernized,” as the aircraft has been upgraded to use an open architecture design, advanced datalinks and a newer propulsion system.
The changes enhance its ability to modify capabilities, resist electronic threats and provide a greater payload capacity and longer flight time than its predecessor.
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

articles.title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
articles.snippet: The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House.
articles.full_text:
The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
A person in Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph).
U.S. pressures Ukraine over refinery attacks
The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections.
But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior U.S. official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.”
The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the U.S. Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X on Wednesday that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment.
Decline in relations
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on Oct. 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. They told Ukrainian officials that the U.S. was frustrated with Kyiv’s continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.
The U.S. delegation also explained Washington’s decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow’s stance on peace talks.
That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to U.S. and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some U.S. lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.
In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Trump criticized each other, with Zelenskiy calling the U.S. decision on the Russian diesel deal “weak.” Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelenskiy’s ouster.
Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. Trump said on Tuesday Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Following the move to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.
The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.

articles.title: South Korean lasers down three drones in Army demo, Hanwha says
articles.snippet: Hanwha Systems laser weapons shot down target drones during a South Korean Army demonstration, the company said.
articles.full_text:
Two laser weapons developed by Hanwha Systems shot down all three target drones during a South Korean Army demonstration on Oct. 14, the company said, as it pitches the technology to foreign buyers.
The company’s stationary Cheongwang laser air defense weapon and a 30-kilowatt-class vehicle-mounted laser took part in the live-fire event, held during the Army’s TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise. About 500 people attended, according to Hanwha, including Army Chief of Staff Gen. Kim Kyu-ha.
Cheongwang fired on a drone overhead that “caught fire and fell from the sky,” The Korea Times reported from the exercise at a training ground in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province. The laser was one part of a layered counter-drone demonstration that also included electronic jamming and a K21 armored vehicle firing on incoming drones.
Hanwha did not say which system destroyed which drones, what kinds of drones were used, what vehicle carries the newer laser or the range of either weapon.
The Oct. 14 demonstration followed a Sept. 16 event at South Korea’s 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition, where Cheongwang downed four drones and two larger unmanned aircraft in succession, Hanwha said.
Cheongwang, meaning “light of the sky,” in Korean is formally known as the Laser Air Defense Weapon Block-I. Hanwha developed it under a program led by South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development. The company calls it the world’s first operationally deployed laser weapon.
South Korea first fielded the system in December 2024 and had about five units at major government facilities as of June, including the Ministry of National Defense building, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.
North Korean drones have repeatedly violated South Korean airspace. In December 2022, five crossed the border, one reaching Seoul. Fighter jets, attack helicopters and warning shots failed to bring any of them down, Defense News reported at the time.
Hanwha says each Cheongwang shot costs about $1.50, in line with the figure South Korea’s arms procurement agency gave in 2024. Unlike guns or missiles, the system uses no ammunition and can continue firing as long as it has power. The company asserts lasers can counter cheap drones used for surveillance and strikes without relying on much costlier missile-based air defenses.
Hanwha is also developing a 50 kW Laser Armored Vehicle in-house for export customers and displayed a model of it at the MSPO defense show in Kielce, Poland, in September.
At the show, Hanwha Systems manager Hyungun Park told Defense News that the company had built a prototype and planned to begin production by the end of 2027. He said Hanwha was in talks with potential buyers in Europe, Asia and the Middle East about exporting Cheongwang.
South Korea’s 2027 defense budget proposal includes funding to begin research on a mobile Block-II version of Cheongwang, UPI reported.
Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

articles.title: Bulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, defense minister says
articles.snippet: Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defenses.
articles.full_text:
Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defenses after a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday.
Drones hit two ships that caught fire off Romania’s Black Sea coast this week. On Tuesday, a commercial vessel sank off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast following a drone attack, prompting Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.
The attacks have highlighted the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict poses to commercial shipping near NATO’s southeastern flank, prompting Bulgaria to push for stronger alliance defenses in the Black Sea.
“We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision,” Stoyanov said.
Stoyanov said he planned to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Romanian President Nicusor Dan on Thursday, saying afterwards that NATO would “continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
Asked about Bulgaria’s request on Friday, a NATO official said the issue would be discussed further by ambassadors from the alliance’s 32 member states next week.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October.

articles.title: Israel secures procurement of 12 Apache gunships in last-minute maneuver
articles.snippet: Israel is set to acquire 12 Apache “Echo” attack helicopters from Boeing, according to an Israeli ministry of defense announcement this week.
articles.full_text:
JERUSALEM — Israel is set to acquire 12 Apache “Echo” attack helicopters from Boeing, according to an Israeli ministry of defense announcement this week.
The deal secures the advanced variant of the helicopter, with scheduled delivery at the beginning of the next decade. It follows months of uncertainty surrounding the deal’s viability, caused by the Israeli government’s inability to finalize the pact despite multiple offer extensions granted by the Americans.
An agreement was previously stalled due to a dispute between the Israeli ministry of finance and the Israeli ministry of defense over funding sources. The ministry of finance demanded budget adjustments and a defined funding source, while the defense establishment pressed to approve the procurement as “urgent,” regardless of general budget discussions.
This gridlock persisted even as the U.S. granted Israel several extensions, culminating in a deadline of Oct. 7, 2026. After missing this original window, concerns arose in Israel that Boeing’s production slot would be routed to other international customers, leading to delivery delays and price increases.
In a last-minute move, Israeli defense officials reached out to their U.S. counterparts and requested another extension. The Americans agreed and opened what Israeli officials conveyed to the press here as a “final window” on the condition that the deal be signed immediately. This prompted an urgent Israeli Cabinet phone vote on Wednesday, which approved the necessary budgetary source at the expense of another long-term, non-defense national program, and made the signing of the deal possible at the same day.
The AH-64E Apache “Echo” is a twin-engine, tandem-seat attack helicopter. The aircraft’s integrated weapon and targeting suite accommodates a payload of up to 16 Hellfire missiles, 76 2.75-inch rockets, and an M230-series 30mm automatic chain gun supplied with up to 1,200 rounds of ammunition.
The platform incorporates digital network connectivity via Link 16, manned-unmanned teaming capabilities for drone control, and a modular open systems approach designed to allow the integration of hardware and software modifications.
Tzally Greenberg is the Israel correspondent for Defense News. He has experience reporting on economic affairs as well as defense and cyber companies.

articles.title: Zone 5 ‘found a spot’ in drone interceptor market with new Eclipse: CEO
articles.snippet: CEO Thomas Akers told Breaking Defense that the company’s recent acquisition by Norwegian defense firm Kongsberg offers “an immediate step change” for the startup firm, whose portfolio now spans from a reusable drone interceptor to a low-cost cruise missile.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Defense startup Zone 5 is joining the rush for counter-drone tech, debuting a new interceptor dubbed the “Eclipse” that the company says can combat high-speed, unmanned threats.
Still in development but shown publicly for the first time at the Association of the United States Army conference here, the Eclipse offers a lower-cost, reusable option to take down high-speed drones, Zone 5 CEO Thomas Akers told Breaking Defense.
Arguing that the market is “coalescing” around smaller interceptors that are in turn challenged by more capable drones, Akers said his firm “found a spot” for a larger interceptor with modular payloads.
Larger doesn’t mean too large — an Eclipse model on display at Zone 5’s booth measured 39 in. long and 32 in. wide. But according to Akers, the platform can sport a high-powered microwave that can zap a drone’s electronics, or can carry a kinetic payload to knock one out of the sky. A company fact sheet said the Eclipse can take off and land vertically, achieve speeds of over 200 knots (230 miles per hour) and reach over 30 miles.
Akers said he expects Eclipse to be in development for roughly another six months before entering production, and is initially aimed at the American market. He said the company is aiming to build hundreds of copies a month but declined to comment on an expected price tag, pointing to various potential payloads that influence a final cost.
Akers explained that the Eclipse helps round out Zone 5’s offerings for layered defenses, from a drone-mounted firearm featured on the firm’s Paladin system to its White Spike anti-air missile. Zone 5’s burgeoning portfolio, which includes a cruise missile dubbed Rusty Dagger exported to Ukraine and on order for the Pentagon, likely helped attract the attention of the Norwegian defense firm Kongsberg, which completed an acquisition of Zone 5 earlier this year.
The Kongsberg acquisition “bring[s] kind of an immediate step change” regarding Zone 5’s access to international resources, Akers said. While Zone 5 still operates separately from Kongsberg in the United States, “globally, we present one unified front under the Kongsberg brand.”
The company’s new Norwegian ownership also “gives us access to a larger portfolio of vendors” that can help expand supply chains beyond the US, Akers added. Looking ahead, he said that the firm is going to remain focused on producing low-cost cruise missiles and technologies that can defeat Group 1-4 drones. A key goal is producing thousands of missiles annually, he said, along with leveraging Kongsberg resources to iterate on Zone 5’s products to increase lethality and survivability.
Alongside recent agreements like a Navy program for maritime strike and a Pentagon-wide effort for containerized munitions, one big opportunity for Zone 5, the Air Force’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) program, is just over the horizon. In the coming years the service plans to acquire tens of thousands of FAMM missiles using multi-year deals, drawing from a pool of vendors including Zone 5, Anduril and CoAspire.
But after using dollars from the One Big Beautiful Bill to kickstart procurement in fiscal 2026, the Air Force once again banked on reconciliation to deliver funds for buying FAMM in FY27 — a prospect dimmed by doubts over another reconciliation bill.
“If multi-year doesn’t happen the way that it’s scheduled to, that sends a clear signal to industry,” Akers said, adding that a shortfall of appropriations means “you’re going to have, definitely, a recoil, and it’s going to be felt beyond just FAMM.”

articles.title: Germany changes course on plans to buy MQ-28 drone wingman: Boeing official
articles.snippet: Germany has set a target of 2029 to field a CCA, which would make it the first European country to reach such a milestone, but that timeline now looks to be in doubt.
articles.full_text:
BELFAST — The German Ministry of Defence has formally notified Boeing that it will not be directly procuring the company’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat drone wingman, as Berlin readjusts plans for a lucrative Collaborative Combat Aircraft procurement.
A spokesperson for the US giant told Breaking Defense today that the ministry had “informed” the company of the move to abandon the aircraft purchase. Berlin’s decision was first reported by Politico.
The Boeing spokesperson deferred comments on why the German Ministry of Defence had ended the Ghost Bat acquisition plan to the ministry.
In a statement to Breaking Defense, a German Ministry of Defence spokesperson said that based on a “matter of principle—and regardless of the specific case in question—we cannot provide information regarding potential procurement projects.”
The spokesperson added, “This is due to regulations concerning procurement and public contracting law, as well as the requirement that such matters first be addressed by parliament.”
The new wingmen will fly alongside fighter jets and carry out strike missions. Germany has set a target of 2029 to field them, which would make it the first European country to reach such a milestone, but that timeline now looks to be in doubt. Politico stated that Berlin will wait until the early 2030s for the capability to arrive, with aircraft tests starting in 2027. The tests are a chance for other competitors and Boeing to fight to be selected for the CCA acquisition.
The Boeing spokesperson explained that the company “stands ready to support” its German customer on next steps.
A host of other airframers are likely to offer their wares, including Germany’s Helsing, pitching the CA-1 Europa. The CCA, according to the firm, is due to be ready for operations by 2029.
Under a partnership between Airbus and US manufacturer Kratos, the U740-Valkyrie is also set to compete to be Germany’s CCA. First flight of the wingman drone was announced on Monday.
“This key milestone confirms that Airbus and Kratos are on track to deliver a combat-ready uncrewed Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) by 2029, addressing the operational requirements of the German and other European Armed Forces,” said the European prime, in a statement at the time.
Further afield, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems could also offer a wingman from its Gambit family. “We have certainly spoken to Germany many, many times about our CCA and what there is to offer,” company spokesperson C. Mark Brinkely told Breaking Defense in June.

articles.title: Open system architecture will be ‘hyper important’ in downselect of Army’s XM30: Senior official
articles.snippet: An open systems architecture allows the Army and its industry partners to plug new and different software and hardware capabilities into the platform.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army will make open systems architecture a key criterion when selecting the winner for its XM30 Optionally Manned Fighting Vehicle, a top official overseeing ground vehicles told Breaking Defense this week.
During an interview at the annual AUSA conference, Brig. Gen. Troy Denomy, portfolio acquisition executive for ground maneuver, said the Army is prioritizing the ability to rapidly adapt its platforms and integrate new technologies as threats evolve — particularly in the counter-unmanned aerial aerial systems fight.
“There’s other aspects that we are absolutely evaluating, but that one is hyper important to me, and we are actually going to evaluate that as part of this selection process,” Denomy added.
The XM30 is intended to replace the Army’s Bradley Fighting Vehicle, which has served as a central component of the service’s armored formations for decades. The next-generation vehicle is being designed to give soldiers improved protection and capabilities to operate against new battlefield threats.
An open systems architecture allows the Army and its industry partners to plug new and different software and hardware capabilities into the platform as emerging tech becomes available and as the threat picture changes, Denomy explained. Out of the two vendors who are competing for the program — American Rheinmetall and General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS) — he said it’s “too early to tell” which company has implemented a more open architecture.
Both vendors have delivered one XM30 prototype each to the Army for testing at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Denomy said. Testing has identified some software capabilities that the vendors need to “tweak,” particularly involving communication between platform subsystems, he said.
“Both vendors are being very responsive to those changes that are necessary,” Denomy said. He added that “it’s nothing atypical for a prototype,” and the open systems architectures for both platforms have allowed the changes to be made quickly.
Though the government is operating under a continuing resolution and Congress has yet to pass the fiscal 2027 budget, Denomy told Breaking Defense that he believes the XM30 program will successfully move forward. He pointed to conversations the service had with congressional staff members at the Army Modernization Days in Aberdeen two weeks ago.
“We spent the whole day with the professional staff members and felt like what we were talking about was positively received of where we are in the program, and that we will be ready based off of our plan to execute the dollars with the appropriation forthcoming,” Denomy said.
The Army requested $547 million to procure 19 XM30s in FY27, as Breaking Defense previously reported. However, the House Appropriations defense subcommittee drafted a version of the FY27 spending bill that reduced the procurement line to just $33.1 million.
Separately, Denomy said that the Army is conducting experimental testing with BAE Systems’ Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle (AMPV) equipped with a 30mm Kongsberg turret — a platform known as the AMPV-30. The vehicle is currently “being exercised in an infantry fighting vehicle role” as part of a Transformation in Contact rotation, he said.
He said there are “significant differences between” what the AMPV-30 and XM30 can do and cautioned against conflating the two vehicles.
The AMPV-30 gives the Army an opportunity to explore an infantry fighting vehicle role for the platform, originally designed as a replacement for the M113 family of armored personnel carriers and support vehicles. Unlike the XM30, which is an Army-funded program, the AMPV-30 is self-funded by BAE Systems.
Denomy praised BAE for investing its own funding to give the Army additional options, saying the effort could allow the AMPV to conduct more types of missions.
“For me what this showcases from an AMPV perspective [are] potential opportunities in the future for other mission roles for it. They do the standard things that are part of the program of record — whether it’s the general purpose, the medical variant [or] the mission command variant. Well, now they’ve demonstrated [a version] with a turret that could fill a role,” he added.
Further, he emphasized that the “commitment behind XM30 is real and it’s important, and we have two very viable offerings.”

articles.title: Proofpoint lines up $6.3 billion deal for Varonis’ data security
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Cybersecurity giant Proofpoint says it will acquire Miami-based data visibility and security company Varonis in an all-cash transaction worth $6.3 billion.
articles.full_text:
Proofpoint lines up $6.3 billion deal for Varonis’ data security
Cybersecurity giant Proofpoint says it will acquire a similarly long-running company, Varonis, in an all-cash transaction worth $6.3 billion.
“The combined company will serve more than 16,000 enterprises and millions of organizations globally, creating one of the world’s leading pure-play cybersecurity companies and establishing the industry's largest data and AI cybersecurity organization,” Proofpoint said in announcing the deal on Thursday.
Miami-based Varonis, founded in 2005, focuses on data visibility and security. The footprint for California-headquartered Proofpoint, founded in 2002, traditionally includes email security and identity threat defense. It’s owned by private equity firm Thoma Bravo.
AI figured prominently in Thursday’s announcement. The goal is to create a platform that “helps organizations adopt AI with confidence: finding and protecting sensitive data, controlling what people and AI can access, and stopping data loss.”
Both companies are known for their cybersecurity research.
Varonis researchers recently got headlines for a report in which they manipulated Microsoft’s AI assistant Copilot Personal into explaining how to hack itself.
Proofpoint analysts published research earlier this month about a high-level, apparently China-backed phishing campaign geared toward espionage.
Other big cybersecurity company moves this year include Accenture’s plan to acquire a majority stake in Dragos as part of a broader $4.175 billion deal involving other companies, and Cyera’s $1 billion acquisition of Oasis Security, which closed in September.
Joe Warminsky
has been the news editor for Recorded Future News since 2022. He has three decades of experience as an editor and writer in the Washington, D.C., area. He previously he helped lead CyberScoop for more than five years. Prior to that, he was a digital editor at WAMU 88.5, the NPR affiliate in Washington, and he spent more than a decade editing coverage of Congress for CQ Roll Call.

articles.title: Moscow police detain suspected DataSuckers hackers linked to breaches in Ukraine and Russia
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Russian authorities have reportedly detained three suspected members of the DataSuckers hacking group following a cyberattack on a popular restaurant chain that exposed vast amounts of customer information.
articles.full_text:
Moscow police detain suspected DataSuckers hackers linked to breaches in Ukraine and Russia
Russian authorities have reportedly detained three suspected members of the DataSuckers hacking group following a cyberattack on a popular restaurant chain that exposed vast amounts of customer information.
A Moscow court on Wednesday placed 19-year-old Denis Fridman under house arrest until December 8 in connection with the Dodo Pizza breach, which reportedly involved the theft of records related to hundreds of millions of orders placed over 15 years. He faces charges connected to the illegal handling of computer information containing personal data.
Fridman is one of four alleged members of DataSuckers, a financially motivated hacking group that has claimed responsibility for recent attacks on major businesses in Russia and Ukraine. Two other suspects have been detained while a fourth remains at large, according to Russian newspaper Kommersant and Telegram news outlet Baza. The suspects reportedly include citizens of Russia, Kazakhstan and Belarus.
According to Baza, police identified the suspected hackers after Fridman accidentally exposed his IP address while accessing data stolen from Dodo Pizza, allowing authorities to trace him to his home in the Russian city of Barnaul.
The attack reportedly began when the hackers discovered Dodo Pizza's corporate credentials exposed on GitHub. Using those credentials, the attackers allegedly gained access to interconnected company systems, including cloud storage and databases, as well as stored passwords.
Kommersant reported that the stolen database was offered for sale on the dark web and that the hackers received $100,000 for the archive, with the money transferred to a shared cryptocurrency wallet. The wallet's password was reportedly changed after Fridman's arrest.
Recorded Future News could not independently verify the circumstances that led Russian law enforcement to the suspects.
Dodo Pizza, a Russian fast-food chain operating approximately 1,500 restaurants across 28 countries, previously acknowledged that attackers may have accessed customer information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth and order details.
Attacks across Russia and Ukraine
DataSuckers has emerged in recent months, claiming responsibility for attacks on major businesses in Russia and Ukraine.
In September, the group claimed responsibility for breaching Russian tour operator Tez Tour, saying it had spent about two weeks inside the company's systems and obtained large amounts of customer information.
The hackers also defaced the company's website. Tez Tour acknowledged the disruption but disputed claims that customer data had been compromised, saying it had isolated its internal systems before the attackers could access them.
Fridman allegedly participated in that attack, according to Kommersant. The newspaper reported that he had previously targeted Ukrainian websites before joining DataSuckers.
Earlier this month, the group claimed responsibility for an attack on ATB, Ukraine's largest grocery store chain, demanding $400,000 and threatening to publish data it claimed to have stolen from millions of customers.
The hackers placed an extortion message and a countdown timer on the retailer's website, which subsequently became unavailable. ATB denied that customer information had been compromised and said it had temporarily taken some online services offline for technical maintenance.
DataSuckers claimed to have obtained records belonging to 7.9 million ATB customers, including names, contact information, addresses and password hashes, as well as employee passport information and more than 11 million order records. Those claims have not been independently verified.
The group describes itself as financially motivated rather than politically aligned. It primarily communicates in Russian and uses a public Telegram channel to announce attacks, publish details of alleged intrusions and invite victims, journalists and law enforcement agencies to contact its members.
In a message posted last weekend, DataSuckers said it was continuing operations but would reduce its public activity.
"We're operating as usual, but you'll be seeing less public activity from us," the group said. "For now, we're focused on specific targets and working on them."
The group has not published any further messages on its Telegram channel since that statement.

articles.title: Baltimore suburb confirms August data breach after ransomware claims
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Anne Arundel County, Maryland, said an intruder stole files from government systems, and investigators are working to assess how much data was exposed.
articles.full_text:
Baltimore suburb confirms August data breach after ransomware claims
Officials in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, confirmed that hackers stole files from government systems during an incident in August.
A county spokesperson told Recorded Future News that they discovered “irregular activity” on August 28 and began an investigation on a “limited subset of systems within the county computer network.”
“Through the course of the county’s response and investigation, it was determined that an unauthorized actor gained access to a limited number of systems and copied certain files from those systems,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson did not respond to questions about what data was involved but said investigators are currently reviewing the files to determine whether any stolen information related to residents of the county.
The Baltimore suburb is home to more than 600,000 residents and the state’s capital of Annapolis. Washington, D.C. is nearby, as well. Dozens of federal agencies have offices or headquarters in the county, including the Defense Department, the Internal Revenue Service, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Social Security Administration, the Department of Agriculture, the U.S. Coast Guard and more.
County officials said they notified federal law enforcement about the data breach as well as other government agencies.
The attack was claimed by the Rhysida ransomware gang, which threatened to leak 2.6 terabytes worth of documents stolen from the county if a $2 million ransom was not paid.
The group recently attempted to extort the government of Berlin after stealing troves of emails and contracts from government systems.
Rhysida has repeatedly targeted governments across the globe since emerging several years ago. Its victims include Kuwait’s Finance Ministry, the city of Seattle and the city of Columbus, Ohio and even the transportation department of Maryland.
Anne Arundel County dealt with a ransomware attack by a different group last year that forced the government to shut off multiple systems.
In a stroke of bad luck, the county released a new statement about last year’s attack on Thursday evening, telling residents that it planned to send out breach notification letters about leaked data in that incident on October 19.
A spokesperson for the county told Recorded Future News that the August 28 attack is a “separate incident.”
The Anne Arundel County spokesperson added that recent reports “indicate that there has been a surge in these kinds of calculated cybercrimes specifically targeting state and local governments.”
Cities and counties in New Mexico, Utah, Texas, Nebraska, Missouri and Arizona have all dealt with service outages over the last two weeks due to cyberattacks.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Suspected Chinese espionage attackers abusing BeyondTrust IT support zero-day
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: An alleged Chinese state-backed group is using a new zero-day affecting BeyondTrust IT support software to conduct espionage attacks.
articles.full_text:
Suspected Chinese espionage attackers abusing BeyondTrust IT support zero-day
An alleged Chinese state-backed group is using a new zero-day in BeyondTrust software to conduct espionage attacks.
BeyondTrust, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed the zero-day on Thursday evening, publishing incident reports detailing attacks involving the bug.
The identity security company said the vulnerability affects its Remote Support appliances that enable IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. A patch has been released addressing the issue and several mitigations are available. Other cybersecurity firms have since confirmed exploitation.
The company said it was first tipped off to the bug — tagged as CVE-2026-102764 — on September 27, when an attack against another vendor's edge appliances became public and sparked an investigation into a similar issue. Mandiant also warned BeyondTrust of a potential vulnerability, sending the company’s engineering team on a hunt that led them back to a zero-day exploited on August 29.
Mandiant incident responders said the attackers were able to escalate their privileges after exploiting the bug, moving laterally within the victim’s network and establishing a deeper foothold.
They noted that the group behind the attacks — which they call Armory Castle or UNC5221 — “leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals” due to their abuse of proprietary tools. Mandiant saw the group use custom malware they call Sawfly and Bareclaw.
The threat actors found a way to get every credential the appliance stored and were able to modify files that survive reboots and configuration resets.
Mandiant warned that any vulnerable appliance that was reachable from the internet should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed.
‘Long-term intelligence collection’
BeyondTrust confirmed Mandiant’s assessment that Armory Castle is a Chinese “state-sponsored espionage operation focused on long-term intelligence collection.”
“ARMORY CASTLE’s documented targets include legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology companies, and government,” the company said, noting that researchers believe the group targets technology firms to help with the discovery of other zero-day exploits.
The group was previously responsible for exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in popular edge devices and was known to use passive backdoors and other novel tools to sustain their access to breached systems.
The group has been active since October 2023 and Google said they have “targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations.”
“In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed,” they said.
“It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764.”
Google compared the situation to previous incidents where the same threat actors conducted widespread exploitation of two bugs affecting products from IT firm Ivanti following their disclosure.
Armory Castle was also previously implicated in exploiting zero-days affecting Citrix as well as multiple issues in Ivanti products, including CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, and CVE-2025-0282.
“In 2025, Mandiant reported that the actor took an Ivanti patch for a flaw that had been rated low risk, studied it, and turned it into working remote code execution against unpatched appliances,” BeyondTrust said.
“The actor uses a zero-day selectively against chosen targets, and once the vulnerability is public, the actor typically moves to broad exploitation of every instance still unpatched.”
Last year, Mandiant and multiple U.S. agencies warned about activity from the group targeting governments, legal firms, software-as-a-service providers and technology companies.

articles.title: Federal bankruptcy courts dealing with outages after contractor cyberattack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The incident, which involved a government contractor, has halted all production of bankruptcy notices.
articles.full_text:
Federal bankruptcy courts dealing with outages after contractor cyberattack
A cyberattack on a U.S. government contractor has impacted the platform used by all federal bankruptcy courts across the country.
The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts published a statement on Thursday afternoon warning that a cyberattack on British multinational BAE Systems disrupted the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) — a system that produces and transmits bankruptcy notices for all federal bankruptcy courts.
“The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts has been in communication with the impacted courts and is also coordinating with BAE Systems. BAE is actively investigating this incident and working to restore operations,” officials said.
“As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service.”
The incident has halted all production of bankruptcy notices as well. The office did not respond to requests for further details about the nature of the incident or whether data was stolen.
BAE Systems is one of the largest defense contractors in the world and is deeply embedded in the U.S. Government — providing aerospace, weapons and information security services across several federal departments.
A spokesperson for the company said they are “aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it.”
“We are coordinating closely with [the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts] on the response,” they added.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which typically handles cyberattacks on federal agencies, directed Recorded Future News to the U.S. Courts. The FBI did not respond to requests for comment.
The attack on the bankruptcy court system comes weeks after Arizona’s state court system was breached and the information of more than 1.3 million people was leaked.
Last year, U.S. federal court officials said they were working to bolster online security for sensitive documents and other case files in an attempt to block cyberattacks and data breaches. The move followed a major hack of the courts’ case filing system which officials feared exposed the identities of confidential informants in criminal cases.
The federal courts docketing system was also attacked by hackers in early 2020.
The U.S. government has been battered by cyberattacks in recent weeks, with incidents involving the Defense Department and the FBI.
On Wednesday, the Department of Transportation confirmed that a safety agency contact center was temporarily taken offline after a contractor was hit with a cyberattack.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.snippet: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
“Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.”

articles.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.snippet: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today's epic patch batch dwarfs September's record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.
Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).
At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.
While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.
Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.
“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.
Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.
“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

articles.title: FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm
articles.snippet: Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested the co-founder of a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.
articles.full_text:
Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.
The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.
One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.
An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.
According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.
[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].
“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.
Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”
The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.
Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”
“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”
Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.
ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.
Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.
Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.
This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.
The irony here is hard to miss. The industry sells “communicating with a criminal isn’t the same as paying” as a clean distinction, but the line between negotiator and middleman gets blurry fast when the same people sit between victims and extortionists. Charges are only allegations at this point, but if the other firms Brian mentions get charged too, expect a lot more scrutiny of how ransomware negotiators operate and who they’re really accountable to.

I think I first ran into it in the early days of the anti-spam efforts, where working solutions were sidelined in favor of poorly functioning technologies that mostly served to give monopoly players control of deliverability. chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:
– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect,

– Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting
thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one
transfer to be useful to the extortion side.
The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside
the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small
repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.
